extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics students, and research-active mathematicians (graduate students, postdocs, faculty)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for creating and managing informal mathematical writeups (sketches of arguments, tricks, incomplete proofs) so they can be recovered, reused, or shared later. Focuses on content level, format, storage, and dissemination practices for research notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write down any interesting argument or trick
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down (preferably on a computer) a sketch of any interesting argument I came across – not necessarily at a publication level of quality, but detailed enough that I could then safely forget about the details, and readily recover the argument from the sketch whenever the need arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record sketches of tricks/arguments as you encounter them rather than relying on memory; the sketch need not be polished or publishable but should capture the core idea so you (or others) can reconstruct it later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer computer-based sketches
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping notes on a computer makes them permanently available, searchable, easier to edit, share, back up, and reuse in future papers, lectures, or proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient detail for later reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Not necessarily at a publication level of quality, but detailed enough that I could then safely forget about the details, and readily recover the argument from the sketch whenever the need arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for 'barely enough details' to reconstruct the entire argument later; a terse but accurate sketch is often more useful than no record at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make informal notes publicly available when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you have written up such a sketch, you might consider making it available (e.g. on your web site), even if it does not rise to the level of originality and depth required for a publishable paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing sketches on a personal website or blog increases discoverability and may aid teaching, collaboration, or future research; do not withhold notes solely because they are informal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record abandoned or incomplete arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have an incomplete (or otherwise unsatisfactory) argument for a problem that you are working on, and you are planning to abandon it, you may still wish to write an informal sketch of it just for yourself (giving barely enough details to allow you to readily reconstruct the whole thing later on), and store it somewhere on your computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even discarded approaches can be valuable later; saving a brief sketch avoids re-deriving the same dead-end and preserves potentially useful ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Back up your notes
rubrics_metrics.description: I also recommend some way of backing up your computer files, e.g., by using a cloud-based file storage system such as Dropbox.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use backups (cloud storage, versioned backups) to ensure your notes are not lost to hardware failure or accidental deletion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use TeX/plain-text formats for collaboration and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: A content-oriented, text-based format such as TeX and its relatives makes more sense [for collaborators and journals].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: journals and arXiv are optimised for TeX; most professional mathematicians use TeX; .sty files simplify conversion to journal formats; plain text facilitates editing, applying house styles, and interoperability with collaborators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer plain-text/version-controlled workflows for collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: It is also easier to collaborate with plain text formats (such as .tex files) than with richer formats for various technical reasons (e.g. one can work on separate sections separately, and use version control software to track changes and edits more effectively).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use section-based editing, version control systems (git, etc.), and textual formats to enable parallel work, track changes, and merge contributions cleanly; network effects favour widely-used formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use WYSIWYG tools only when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A custom WYSIWYG editor is appropriate for single-author, self-published articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WYSIWYG editors can be fine for solo, informal writing, but are less suitable for collaborative projects or formal publication because import/export and collaboration tooling are weaker; if using WYSIWYG, ensure export to journal-friendly formats is feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing practice improves technical and expository skill
rubrics_metrics.description: It gives you practice in mathematical writing, both at the technical level (e.g. in learning how to use TeX) and at an expository or pedagogical level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly writing sketches builds competence with typesetting and exposition, which benefits future papers, lecture notes, proposals, and teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing notes tests understanding and frees cognitive load
rubrics_metrics.description: It tests whether you have really understood the argument on more than just a superficial level. It frees up mental space; you no longer have to remember the exact details of the argument, and so can devote your memory to learning newer topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use note-writing as a self-check for comprehension and as an external memory to reduce cognitive burden and enable faster learning of new material.
